items.title: Evolution & Committees on Panchayati Raj
items.body:
**In one line**
Local self-government in India grew from British-era experiments and a string of expert committees before it finally won a place in the Constitution in 1992.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC/UPSC repeatedly test "which committee recommended what" and "who started local self-government", so the sequence and the key names are high-value.

**The story**
- **British roots**: **Mayo's Resolution (1870)** began financial decentralisation; **Lord Ripon's Resolution (1882)** — the **'Magna Carta' of local self-government** — mandated elected members and non-official chairpersons. The **Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1907)**, chaired by **C.E.H. Hobhouse**, stressed village panchayats, and the **Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms (1919)** made local government a transferred provincial subject.
- **After independence**: **Article 40 (a Directive Principle)** directed the State to organise village panchayats, but being non-justiciable it produced no uniformity, and **B.R. Ambedkar** was sceptical of panchayats. The **Community Development Programme (1952)** and **National Extension Service (1953)** underperformed for lack of people's participation.
- **The committees** that shaped reform:

| Committee | Year | Core recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Balwant Rai Mehta | 1957 | **Three-tier** PRI (Village–Block–District) |
| Ashok Mehta | 1977 | **Two-tier** (Zilla Parishad + Mandal Panchayat) |
| G.V.K. Rao | 1985 | District as the **basic unit of planning** |
| L.M. Singhvi | 1986 | **Constitutional status** for PRIs |
| P.K. Thungon | 1989 | Constitutional recognition |

**Rajasthan** launched PRIs first (**2 October 1959**, Nagaur), followed by **Andhra Pradesh (1 November 1959)**.

**Terms explained**
- **Decentralisation** — handing powers and funds down from the Centre/State to local bodies.
- **Directive Principle (DPSP)** — a goal the Constitution asks the State to pursue, but which courts cannot enforce.
- **Non-justiciable** — not enforceable in a court.

**Don't confuse**
- **Balwant Rai Mehta = three-tier; Ashok Mehta = two-tier** — do not swap them.
- **L.M. Singhvi (constitutional status)** vs **G.V.K. Rao (district planning)** — a frequent match-the-pair trap.

**Remember it**
Committee order by year: Balwant ('57) → Ashok ('77) → GVK Rao ('85) → Singhvi ('86) → Thungon ('89).

**TL;DR**
- Ripon 1882 = 'Magna Carta' of local self-government; Mayo 1870 began financial decentralisation.
- Article 40 (DPSP) directed village panchayats; non-justiciable.
- Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) = three-tier; Ashok Mehta (1977) = two-tier; Singhvi (1986) = constitutional status.
- Rajasthan launched PRIs first (2 Oct 1959), then Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1959).
keyPoints: Ripon's Resolution of 1882 is the 'Magna Carta' of local self-government; Mayo's 1870 Resolution began financial decentralisation.
Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1907) was chaired by C.E.H. Hobhouse.
Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organise village panchayats; it is non-justiciable.
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier system; Ashok Mehta (1977) the two-tier system.
L.M. Singhvi (1986) recommended constitutional status for PRIs.
Rajasthan launched PRIs first (2 Oct 1959), followed by Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1959).

items.title: 73rd & 74th Amendments — Structure, Reservation, Tenure
items.body:
**In one line**
Two 1992 amendments — the 73rd for villages and the 74th for towns — finally made local governments a permanent, elected third tier of India's federal system.

**Why it is asked**
The Part/Schedule/Article numbers, the 29-vs-18 figures and the reservation and tenure rules are among the most heavily tested polity facts.

**The story**
- **73rd Amendment** → **Part IX ('The Panchayats')**, Articles **243–243O**, the **Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)**. In force **24 April 1993** (National Panchayati Raj Day).
- **74th Amendment** → **Part IXA ('The Municipalities')**, Articles **243P–243ZG**, the **Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects)**. In force **1 June 1993**.
- **Structure**: three tiers — Village (**Gram Panchayat**) → Intermediate (**Block/Mandal/Taluk**) → District (**Zilla Parishad**). The intermediate tier is **optional** for a State with population **not exceeding 20 lakh** (Art 243B). The **Gram Sabha** (Art 243A) — all registered voters of a village — is the base deliberative unit, and all seats are filled by **direct election** (Art 243C).
- **Reservation and tenure**: **SC/ST** seats are reserved **in proportion to population**; **women** get **not less than one-third** of seats and chairperson posts (Art 243D), and many States, including AP, have raised this to **50%**. Panchayats have a **five-year term** (Art 243E), with elections before expiry or within **6 months** of dissolution. Elections are run by the **State Election Commission** (Art 243K), NOT the Election Commission of India.

**Terms explained**
- **Eleventh / Twelfth Schedule** — lists of subjects the State *may* hand to panchayats (29) and municipalities (18).
- **Gram Sabha** — the village assembly of all adult voters.
- **State Election Commission** — a State body that runs local-body polls.

**Don't confuse**
- **73rd = Rural / 29 subjects / Eleventh Schedule** vs **74th = Urban / 18 subjects / Twelfth Schedule** — do not flip the numbers.
- **State Election Commission (local bodies) is NOT the Election Commission of India** (Parliament/Assembly polls).

**Remember it**
73 = Rural (Panchayats, 11th Schedule, 29); 74 = Urban (Municipalities, 12th Schedule, 18).

**TL;DR**
- 73rd: Part IX, Arts 243–243O, Eleventh Schedule (29), in force 24 Apr 1993.
- 74th: Part IXA, Arts 243P–243ZG, Twelfth Schedule (18), in force 1 Jun 1993.
- Three tiers; intermediate tier optional below 20 lakh population (Art 243B).
- Women ≥ one-third (Art 243D); 5-year term (Art 243E); State Election Commission conducts polls (Art 243K).
keyPoints: 73rd Amendment = Part IX, Arts 243–243O, Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects), in force 24 Apr 1993.
74th Amendment = Part IXA, Arts 243P–243ZG, Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects), in force 1 Jun 1993.
Three-tier structure; intermediate tier optional for states with population ≤ 20 lakh (Art 243B).
One-third of seats and chairperson posts reserved for women (Art 243D); SC/ST reservation is population-proportional.
Panchayats have a five-year term (Art 243E); elections run by the State Election Commission (Art 243K).

items.title: Articles 243–243ZG & the Schedules — Quick Reference
items.body:
**In one line**
Parts IX and IXA pack the whole local-government scheme into a short run of numbered Articles, and the exam picks single Articles out of this list.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-Article questions (243A, 243D, 243I, 243K, 243ZD) are common, so you must be able to attach each number to its provision.

**The story**
The Constitution assigns one job to each Article so that powers, elections and finances all have a clear home.

Panchayats — **Part IX (Arts 243–243O)**:

| Article | Provision |
|---|---|
| 243A | Gram Sabha |
| 243B | Constitution of Panchayats (3 tiers) |
| 243C | Composition |
| 243D | Reservation of seats (SC/ST/women) |
| 243E | Duration — 5 years |
| 243G | Powers, authority and responsibilities; panchayats prepare plans for economic development and social justice |
| 243H | Power to levy and collect taxes, only as authorised by the State Legislature; funds |
| 243I | State Finance Commission |
| 243K | State Election Commission |
| 243M | Part not to apply to certain (Scheduled) areas |

Municipalities — **Part IXA (Arts 243P–243ZG)**:

| Article | Provision |
|---|---|
| 243Q | Three types of municipalities |
| 243R | Composition |
| 243T | Reservation of seats |
| 243W | Powers and functions |
| 243Y | State Finance Commission (municipalities) |
| 243ZA | Elections (State Election Commission) |
| 243ZD | District Planning Committee |
| 243ZE | Metropolitan Planning Committee |

The **Eleventh Schedule** carries 29 functional items for panchayats; the **Twelfth Schedule** carries 18 for municipalities.

**Terms explained**
- **State Finance Commission (243I/243Y)** — reviews, every five years, how money is shared with local bodies.
- **District Planning Committee (243ZD)** — merges the plans of panchayats and municipalities in a district.
- **Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE)** — the same idea for a large metro area.

**Don't confuse**
- **243I = State Finance Commission** vs **243K = State Election Commission** — money versus elections.
- **243ZD (District Planning)** vs **243ZE (Metropolitan Planning)** — district versus metro.

**Remember it**
A-B-C-D-E … I, K: gram-sabhA, Bodies, Composition, reservation-D, duration-E, finance-I, election-K.

**TL;DR**
- 243A = Gram Sabha; 243B = three tiers; 243D = reservation; 243E = 5-year duration.
- 243G = powers/planning; 243H = taxes; 243I = State Finance Commission; 243K = State Election Commission.
- 243ZD = District Planning Committee; 243ZE = Metropolitan Planning Committee.
- Eleventh Schedule = 29 (panchayats); Twelfth Schedule = 18 (municipalities).
keyPoints: 243A = Gram Sabha; 243B = constitution of the three tiers.
243D = reservation; 243E = five-year duration; 243G = powers/planning; 243H = taxes.
243I = State Finance Commission; 243K = State Election Commission for panchayats.
243ZD = District Planning Committee; 243ZE = Metropolitan Planning Committee (Part IXA).
Eleventh Schedule = 29 subjects (panchayats); Twelfth Schedule = 18 subjects (municipalities).
items.mnemonic: 'A B C D E … I K' — Gram sabhA, Bodies, Composition, reservation-D, duration-E, finance-I, election-K.

items.title: PESA Act 1996 & Scheduled Areas
items.body:
**In one line**
PESA, 1996 carries the panchayat system into India's tribal (Fifth Schedule) areas, but reshapes it so that the Gram Sabha — not the higher tiers — holds real power.

**Why it is asked**
The Fifth-vs-Sixth Schedule distinction and "what PESA empowers the Gram Sabha to do" are classic traps.

**The story**
Ordinary **Part IX does not automatically apply to the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled) areas (Article 243M)**, because tribal society needs rules fitted to its customs. Parliament therefore passed the **Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA)**.

PESA extends panchayat provisions to **Fifth Schedule areas across ten States** (including **Andhra Pradesh**) and makes the **Gram Sabha the centre of tribal self-governance**. The Gram Sabha approves development plans and beneficiary lists, manages **minor forest produce, minor water bodies and land**, must be consulted before land acquisition and resettlement, and safeguards **tribal customs and traditions**. PESA also stops higher-tier panchayats from encroaching on the powers of lower tiers.

Several regions stay **outside Part IX**: Fifth Schedule areas (covered instead by PESA), **Sixth Schedule** tribal areas of the North-East, the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram, and hill areas such as Darjeeling.

**Terms explained**
- **Fifth Schedule** — the Constitution's framework for Scheduled areas in mainland States (where PESA applies).
- **Sixth Schedule** — a separate framework for tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (autonomous district councils).
- **Minor forest produce** — non-timber forest items (bamboo, tendu leaves, honey) that tribals may own and sell.

**Don't confuse**
- **PESA covers the Fifth Schedule, NOT the Sixth Schedule** (North-East) — the single most common error.
- PESA aims at **self-governance within the State**, not at creating autonomous regions.

**Remember it**
PESA = Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas — Fifth (not Sixth) Schedule.

**TL;DR**
- Part IX does not automatically apply to Fifth Schedule areas (Art 243M).
- PESA, 1996 extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas in ten States, including AP.
- It makes the Gram Sabha central to tribal self-rule and resource/custom protection.
- PESA = Fifth Schedule; the Sixth Schedule (North-East) is a different system.
keyPoints: Part IX does not automatically apply to Fifth Schedule areas (Article 243M).
PESA Act, 1996 = Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act.
PESA extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas in ten states, including Andhra Pradesh.
It makes the Gram Sabha central to tribal self-rule and protection of customs and resources.
PESA covers the Fifth Schedule, NOT the Sixth Schedule (North-East) areas.
items.mnemonic: PESA = Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas — Fifth (not Sixth) Schedule.

items.title: Urban Local Bodies (74th Amendment)
items.body:
**In one line**
The 74th Amendment gives towns and cities their own elected governments, graded by size from a Nagar Panchayat up to a Municipal Corporation.

**Why it is asked**
The three types under Article 243Q, the Twelfth Schedule figure and the "first corporation" fact are standard one-mark questions.

**The story**
Urban self-government rests on **Part IXA** and the **Twelfth Schedule (18 items)**; India's first municipal corporation was set up at **Madras in 1688**. **Article 243Q** classifies municipalities into three types by the size of the area:

| Body | Constituted for | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **Nagar Panchayat** | Area **in transition** from rural to urban | Chairperson |
| **Municipal Council** | Smaller urban area | President / Chairperson |
| **Municipal Corporation** | Larger urban area | Mayor |

Besides these elected bodies, several **administrative urban bodies** exist outside Art 243Q: the **Notified Area Committee** (a developing town, with all members nominated), **Town Area Committee** (a small town, limited powers), **Cantonment Board** (set up and controlled by the **central government** for the civilian population near military stations), **Township**, **Port Trust** and **Special Purpose Agency**.

Two planning bodies tie the levels together: the **District Planning Committee (Art 243ZD)** consolidates panchayat and municipal plans, and the **Metropolitan Planning Committee (Art 243ZE)** does this for metros with a population of 10 lakh or more.

**Terms explained**
- **Nagar Panchayat** — the municipal body for a place turning from rural into urban.
- **Cantonment Board** — a civic body for a military-station town, run under the central government.
- **Metropolitan area** — an urban area of 10 lakh or more people spread over one or more districts.

**Don't confuse**
- **Nagar Panchayat (transitional area) vs Gram Panchayat (village)** — one is urban-in-the-making, the other is rural.
- **Only a Municipal Corporation is headed by a Mayor**; the smaller bodies have Chairpersons/Presidents.

**Remember it**
Urban ladder by size: Nagar Panchayat < Municipal Council < Municipal Corporation.

**TL;DR**
- Part IXA + Twelfth Schedule (18 items); first corporation at Madras, 1688.
- Article 243Q: Nagar Panchayat (transitional), Municipal Council (smaller), Municipal Corporation (larger, Mayor).
- Cantonment Boards are controlled by the central government.
- 243ZD (District) and 243ZE (Metropolitan) Planning Committees integrate area plans.
keyPoints: Part IXA + Twelfth Schedule (18 items) govern municipalities; first corporation at Madras, 1688.
Article 243Q gives three types: Nagar Panchayat (transitional), Municipal Council (smaller), Municipal Corporation (larger).
A Municipal Corporation is headed by a Mayor.
Cantonment Boards are set up and controlled by the central government.
District Planning Committee (243ZD) and Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE) integrate area plans.
items.mnemonic: Urban ladder by size: Nagar Panchayat < Municipal Council < Municipal Corporation.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — PR Act 1994, Mandal System & Sachivalayams
items.body:
**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh runs a three-tier panchayat system under its 1994 Act and has added the Grama/Ward Sachivalayam layer (2019) to bring government services to people's doorsteps.

**Why it is asked**
AP-specific institutions — the mandal tier, the 1994 Act and the Sachivalayam-Volunteer model — are prime material for the APPSC State paper.

**The story**
- **AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (Act 13 of 1994)** consolidated the State's laws on Gram Panchayats, Mandal Parishads and Zilla Parishads and gave effect to the **73rd Amendment**. AP's three tiers are **Gram Panchayat (Sarpanch) → Mandal Praja Parishad (President) → Zilla Praja Parishad (Chairperson)**. The **mandal** replaced the older block/taluk as the intermediate tier in AP, introduced in the 1980s under **N.T. Rama Rao**.
- **Grama/Ward Sachivalayam system (2019)**: launched on **2 October 2019** for corruption-free, doorstep governance. About **15,004 Grama Sachivalayams** (rural) and **3,842 Ward Sachivalayams** (urban) were set up, each staffed by dedicated functionaries delivering hundreds of government services locally. They are backed by **Grama/Ward Volunteers**, each serving roughly **50 households**, for last-mile delivery of welfare (Direct Benefit Transfer) schemes. This layer is **administrative** and complements — it does **not** replace — the constitutional **Gram Sabha / Panchayat**.
- AP also has **Fifth Schedule areas**, so **PESA, 1996** applies in its tribal (Scheduled) regions.
- **Districts and Zilla Praja Parishads**: Andhra Pradesh has had **28 districts since 31 December 2025**, when **Polavaram** and **Markapuram** became the newest districts. Because there is **one Zilla Praja Parishad per district**, the number of ZPPs follows the number of districts: the **28 Zilla Praja Parishads came into effect on 25 September 2026**, each headed by an elected **Chairperson**.
- **Reservation**: the Constitution guarantees women at least one-third of seats; Andhra Pradesh has **enhanced reservation for women to 50%** in panchayats and municipalities. SC/ST seats remain in proportion to their population in the local-body area.
- **Urban bodies**: municipalities and municipal councils in AP are governed mainly by the **Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965**; large cities have municipal corporations, such as the **Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC)**, one of the largest in the State.
- **Who runs the department**: in the cabinet formed on **12 June 2024**, the **Panchayat Raj and Rural Development** portfolio is held by **Deputy Chief Minister Konidela Pawan Kalyan**.

**Terms explained**
- **Mandal Praja Parishad** — AP's intermediate (block-level) tier, headed by an MPP President.
- **Grama Sachivalayam** — a village secretariat of government staff for single-window service delivery.
- **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** — paying welfare benefits straight into a beneficiary's bank account.

**Don't confuse**
- A **Gram Panchayat is headed by a Sarpanch**, not a Mayor (a Mayor heads a municipal corporation).
- The **Sachivalayam is an administrative layer**; it does not abolish the elected Gram Sabha/Panchayat.
- AP **does have municipal corporations** (for example GVMC) as well as municipalities — not only municipalities.

**Remember it**
AP tiers G-M-Z: Gram → Mandal → Zilla; the Sachivalayam started on Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October 2019.

**TL;DR**
- AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 implemented the 73rd Amendment; tiers = Gram Panchayat → Mandal Praja Parishad → Zilla Praja Parishad.
- The mandal is AP's intermediate tier, from the 1980s under N.T. Rama Rao.
- Grama/Ward Sachivalayam (2 Oct 2019): ~15,004 Grama + 3,842 Ward secretariats, Volunteers for ~50 households each.
- It is administrative and does not replace the Gram Sabha; PESA applies in AP's Fifth Schedule areas.
keyPoints: AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (Act 13 of 1994) implemented the 73rd Amendment and consolidated PRI laws in the state.
AP's three tiers: Gram Panchayat (Sarpanch), Mandal Praja Parishad (President), Zilla Praja Parishad (Chairperson).
The mandal is AP's intermediate tier, introduced in the 1980s under N.T. Rama Rao.
The Grama/Ward Sachivalayam system was launched on 2 October 2019 for doorstep governance.
About 15,004 Grama and 3,842 Ward Sachivalayams operate, backed by Volunteers each serving ~50 households.
The Sachivalayam is administrative and does not replace the constitutional Gram Sabha; PESA applies in AP's Fifth Schedule areas.
AP has 28 districts since 31 Dec 2025 (Polavaram, Markapuram newest); one Zilla Praja Parishad per district — 28 ZPPs effective 25 Sep 2026.

Women's reservation in AP local bodies raised to 50%; urban bodies under the AP Municipalities Act, 1965 (GVMC among the largest corporations); PR & RD portfolio: DyCM Pawan Kalyan (cabinet of 12 Jun 2024).

items.title: PYQ Precision — Age, Tenure & SVAMITVA
items.body:
**In one line**
A few precise facts — the minimum age of 21, the "remainder of term" rule, and the drone-based SVAMITVA scheme — decide several previous-year questions.

**Why it is asked**
These are direct UPSC/APPSC previous-year items where one swapped number (21 vs 25) or one wrong ministry flips the answer.

**The story**
- **Age and tenure**: the **minimum age to be a Panchayat member is 21 years** (Art 243F) — NOT 25 (25 is for the Lok Sabha). The **term is 5 years** (Art 243E), with elections within **6 months** of dissolution. A Panchayat reconstituted after **premature dissolution** serves only the **remainder** of the original term; one that completes its full term gets a fresh 5 years.
- **SVAMITVA Scheme (2020–21)**: the name stands for **S**urvey of **V**illages **A**nd **M**apping with **I**mprovised **T**echnology in **V**illage **A**reas. It uses **drones** to survey **abadi (inhabited) rural land** and issues **property cards** (a record of rights) to household owners. It is implemented by the **Ministry of Panchayati Raj**, and the property cards help owners access institutional credit and reduce land disputes.

**Terms explained**
- **Abadi land** — the inhabited (built-up) part of a village, as opposed to farmland.
- **Property card** — an official document proving ownership of a house/plot.
- **Record of rights** — the government's register of who owns which land.

**Don't confuse**
- **Panchayat member minimum age = 21** (Art 243F), not 25.
- A Panchayat after **premature dissolution** serves only the **leftover term**, not a fresh five years.
- **SVAMITVA is run by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj**, not the Ministry of Rural Development.

**Remember it**
21 to stand for a Panchayat; SVAMITVA = drones + property cards under the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.

**TL;DR**
- Minimum age to be a Panchayat member = 21 years (Art 243F).
- Term = 5 years (Art 243E); elections within 6 months of dissolution.
- After premature dissolution, a Panchayat serves only the remainder of the original term.
- SVAMITVA (2020-21): drones survey abadi land and issue property cards; run by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
keyPoints: Minimum age to be a Panchayat member is 21 years (Art 243F), not 25.
Panchayat term is 5 years (Art 243E); elections within 6 months of dissolution.
A body reconstituted after premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the original term.
SVAMITVA (2020-21) uses drones to survey abadi land and issues property cards.
SVAMITVA is implemented by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
items.source: UPSC 2016 Prelims (Rau's IAS COMPASS); Constitution Arts 243E/243F; Ministry of Panchayati Raj / PIB (SVAMITVA)

items.title: Local Self-Government — Ancient Roots to the 73rd Amendment, Every Committee
items.body:
## From the village sabha to Part IX

**In one line:** village self-rule is ancient, British resolutions (1870, 1882) revived it in modern form, and a chain of committees from **1957** to **1988** led to the **73rd Amendment (1992)**.

**Why it is asked:** committee-recommendation matching and "first state to adopt Panchayati Raj" appear almost every year.

**The story**

### Ancient and medieval
- The **Rigveda** mentions **Sabha, Samiti and Vidatha**; the **Shanti Parva** of the Mahabharata, the **Manusmriti** and **Kautilya's Arthashastra** describe village self-rule.
- The Mahabharata's officials: **Gramik** (one village), **Dashap** (ten), **Vinshya Adhipati** (twenty), **Shat Gram Adhyaksha** (hundred), **Shat Gram Pati** (thousand).
- Gupta period: the district official was the **Vishaya Pati** and the village headman the **Grampati**; Sultanate villages had the **Mukkaddam**, **Patwari** and **Choudhri**.

### British period
| Year | Step |
|---|---|
| **1870** | **Lord Mayo's Resolution** — financial decentralisation |
| **1882** | **Lord Ripon's Resolution** — elected members, non-official chairmen; the **Magna Carta** of local self-government; Ripon is called the **father of local self-government** |
| **1907** | **Royal Commission on Decentralisation** under **C.E.H. Hobhouse** — stressed village panchayats |
| **1919** | **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms** — local government a **transferred** provincial subject |
| **1925** | Eight provinces and six princely states had passed Panchayat Acts |

### After independence
- **Article 40** (a Directive Principle) asks the state to organise village panchayats; **Ambedkar** was sceptical of the village as a unit.
- **Community Development Programme** — **2 October 1952**, inspired by the **Etawah** project of **Albert Mayer**; **National Extension Service** — **1953**.

### The committees
| Committee | Year | Key recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **Balwant Rai Mehta** | **1957** (set up by the **NDC**) | **Three tiers** — village panchayat, panchayat samiti, zilla parishad; "**democratic decentralisation**"; village panchayat directly elected, upper tiers indirectly; samiti the **executive** body, zilla parishad **advisory**, chaired by the **Collector**; NDC accepted it in **January 1958** |
| **Ashok Mehta** | **1977** (Janata government) | **Two tiers** — **zilla parishad** and **mandal panchayat** (a group of villages with **15,000-20,000** people); the **district** as the first point of decentralisation; open participation of **political parties**; compulsory taxation powers; **nyaya panchayats** |
| **G.V.K. Rao** | **1985** | PRIs had become "**grass without roots**"; the **district** as the basic unit of planning; a District Development Commissioner |
| **L.M. Singhvi** | **1986** | **Constitutional recognition**; nyaya panchayats; more finances |
| **P.K. Thungon** | **1988** | Constitutional recognition; the **zilla parishad as the pivot**; the **Collector** as its chief executive |
| **Gadgil** | **1988** | Three tiers, five-year term, reservations, and the ideas of a **State Finance Commission** and **State Election Commission** |
- **Rajasthan** inaugurated Panchayati Raj first at **Nagaur** on **2 October 1959** (by **Nehru**); **Andhra Pradesh** followed on **1 November 1959**.

### The road to the 73rd Amendment
- **64th Amendment Bill (1989)** under **Rajiv Gandhi** passed the Lok Sabha but **failed in the Rajya Sabha**; the V.P. Singh government's bill lapsed.
- The **Narasimha Rao** government's bill became the **73rd Amendment Act, 1992**; it came into force on **24 April 1993** — **National Panchayati Raj Day**. The **Ministry of Panchayati Raj** was created in **2004**.
- The **2nd ARC** sixth report, "**Local Governance — An Inspiring Journey into the Future**", urged **subsidiarity** and **activity mapping**. The source calls the result "**multi-level federalism**".

## Don't confuse
- Balwant Rai Mehta — **three** tiers; Ashok Mehta — **two** tiers.
- G.V.K. Rao — "grass without roots", district planning; L.M. Singhvi — constitutional status.

**TL;DR**
- Mayo 1870 → Ripon 1882 (Magna Carta) → Hobhouse 1907 → 1919 transferred subject.
- CDP 1952 → Balwant Rai Mehta 1957 → Rajasthan 1959 → Ashok Mehta 1977 → G.V.K. Rao 1985 → Singhvi 1986 → Thungon, Gadgil 1988 → 64th Bill 1989 → 73rd Act 1992.
keyPoints: The Rigveda mentions Sabha, Samiti and Vidatha; the Gupta district official was the Vishaya Pati and the village headman the Grampati.
Lord Ripon, whose 1882 Resolution is the Magna Carta of local self-government, is called the father of local self-government.
The Community Development Programme began on 2 October 1952, inspired by Albert Mayer's Etawah project; the National Extension Service followed in 1953.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was set up by the NDC in 1957 and recommended democratic decentralisation with the Collector chairing the zilla parishad.
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) proposed mandal panchayats for 15,000-20,000 people and open participation of political parties.
G.V.K. Rao (1985) called PRIs "grass without roots"; P.K. Thungon (1988) made the zilla parishad the pivot; the 64th Amendment Bill (1989) failed in the Rajya Sabha.

items.title: Part IX Article by Article — Articles 243 to 243O, Compulsory & Voluntary Provisions
items.body:
## The panchayat chapter in detail

**In one line:** Part IX fixes a common frame — Gram Sabha, three tiers, direct elections, reservations, five-year terms, a State Election Commission and a State Finance Commission — and leaves powers and money to state law.

**Why it is asked:** single Articles, the age of **21**, and "which provision is compulsory" are classic UPSC traps (2016, 2013).

**The story**

### Articles 243-243O
| Article | Rule |
|---|---|
| **243** | Definitions — Gram Sabha, panchayat, village, intermediate level |
| **243A** | **Gram Sabha** — all persons on the electoral roll of a village; powers as state law provides |
| **243B** | **Three tiers**; the intermediate tier may be skipped in a state of **not more than 20 lakh** people |
| **243C** | All seats filled by **direct election**; chairpersons of the **intermediate and district** panchayats elected **indirectly** from among members; the village chairperson as state law decides; state law may give seats to **MPs and MLAs** |
| **243D** | Seats for **SCs and STs** in proportion to population; **not less than one-third** for **women** (including SC/ST women); chairperson posts reserved likewise, by **rotation**; reservation for **backward classes** optional |
| **243E** | **Five-year** term from the first meeting; election before expiry or **within six months** of dissolution; a body elected after premature dissolution serves only the **remainder** of the term |
| **243F** | Disqualifications; minimum age **21** (not 25) |
| **243G** | Powers to prepare plans for **economic development and social justice**, including the **Eleventh Schedule** subjects |
| **243H** | Taxes, duties, tolls and fees only as the **state legislature** authorises; grants-in-aid |
| **243I** | **State Finance Commission** by the **Governor** every **five years**; its report and action taken go to the state legislature |
| **243J** | **Audit** of panchayat accounts by state law |
| **243K** | **State Election Commission** — appointed by the **Governor**; removed only like an **HC judge** |
| **243L** | Application to **UTs** as the **President** directs |
| **243M** | Not applicable to **Fifth Schedule** (Scheduled) and tribal areas, **Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram**, hill areas of **Manipur** with district councils and the **Darjeeling** hill areas; Parliament may extend it |
| **243N** | Existing laws continue for **one year** |
| **243O** | **Bar on courts** in electoral matters; disputes only by **election petition** |
- **Art 280(3)(bb)** (added by the 73rd) lets the **Finance Commission** suggest measures to augment state funds for panchayats.

### Compulsory and voluntary provisions
| Compulsory | Voluntary (left to the state) |
|---|---|
| Gram Sabha; three tiers; **direct elections**; indirect election of intermediate and district chairpersons; minimum age **21**; SC/ST and **one-third women** reservation; five-year term and fresh election within six months; **State Election Commission**; **State Finance Commission** | Seats for **MPs and MLAs**; reservation for **backward classes**; financial powers to levy taxes; devolution of **Eleventh Schedule** subjects; autonomy and functions |

## Don't confuse
- **243I** — State Finance Commission; **243K** — State Election Commission. The State Finance Commission's advice is **not binding** on the state government.
- Minimum age **21** for a panchayat seat; **25** is for the Lok Sabha (UPSC 2016).

**TL;DR**
- 243A Gram Sabha; 243B tiers (20 lakh); 243C direct elections; 243D reservation; 243E five years; 243F age 21.
- 243G plans; 243H taxes; 243I SFC; 243J audit; 243K SEC; 243L UTs; 243M exempt areas; 243N one year; 243O courts barred.
keyPoints: Under Article 243C chairpersons of intermediate and district panchayats are elected indirectly from among their members, and state law may give seats to MPs and MLAs.
Article 243D reserves chairperson posts for SCs, STs and women by rotation; reservation for backward classes is left to the states.
Article 243J covers audit of panchayat accounts, 243L application to UTs and 243N continuance of existing laws for one year.
Article 243M exempts Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Fifth Schedule areas, the hill areas of Manipur and Darjeeling.
The 73rd Amendment added Article 280(3)(bb) so that the Finance Commission suggests measures to augment state funds for panchayats.
Compulsory provisions include the Gram Sabha, three tiers, direct elections, one-third women's reservation, the SEC and the SFC; seats for MPs and MLAs and OBC reservation are voluntary.

items.title: Eleventh & Twelfth Schedules Item by Item, and PESA 1996 in Full
items.body:
## What local bodies may do, and the tribal extension

**In one line:** the **Eleventh Schedule** lists **29** subjects for panchayats and the **Twelfth Schedule** **18** for municipalities; **PESA, 1996** extends Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with a powerful Gram Sabha.

**Why it is asked:** "which of these is in the Eleventh/Twelfth Schedule" and "which is NOT an objective of PESA" (UPSC 2013) are frequent.

**The story**

### Eleventh Schedule (Art 243G) — 29 items
| # | Items |
|---|---|
| 1-7 | **Agriculture** and extension; land improvement and **land reforms**; **minor irrigation** and watershed development; **animal husbandry**, dairying, poultry; **fisheries**; **social forestry** and farm forestry; **minor forest produce** |
| 8-15 | **Small-scale industries** including food processing; **khadi**, village and cottage industries; **rural housing**; **drinking water**; **fuel and fodder**; roads, culverts, bridges, **ferries** and waterways; **rural electrification**; **non-conventional energy** |
| 16-22 | **Poverty alleviation**; **education** including primary and secondary schools; technical training and **vocational education**; **adult and non-formal education**; **libraries**; **cultural activities**; **markets and fairs** |
| 23-29 | **Health and sanitation** including hospitals and PHCs; **family welfare**; **women and child development**; social welfare including the handicapped; welfare of **weaker sections**, especially SCs and STs; **public distribution system**; **maintenance of community assets** |

### Twelfth Schedule (Art 243W) — 18 items
| # | Items |
|---|---|
| 1-6 | **Urban planning** including town planning; regulation of **land use** and construction of buildings; planning for economic and social development; **roads and bridges**; **water supply** for domestic, industrial and commercial use; public health, sanitation and **solid waste management** |
| 7-12 | **Fire services**; **urban forestry** and the environment; safeguarding **weaker sections**; **slum improvement**; **urban poverty alleviation**; parks, gardens and **playgrounds** |
| 13-18 | Cultural, educational and aesthetic aspects; **burials and cremation grounds**; **cattle pounds** and prevention of cruelty to animals; **vital statistics** including registration of births and deaths; street lighting, parking lots and bus stops; regulation of **slaughter houses and tanneries** |
- Only the Twelfth Schedule has **fire services**, **slaughter houses**, **cattle pounds** and **vital statistics**; only the Eleventh has **libraries**, **markets and fairs**, the **PDS** and **minor forest produce**.

### PESA, 1996
- **Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act** — passed on the **Dilip Singh Bhuria Committee**'s advice, in force from **24 December 1996**.
- Applies to Fifth Schedule areas in **ten states**: **Andhra Pradesh**, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan and **Telangana**.
- The **Gram Sabha** approves plans and selects beneficiaries; must be **consulted before land acquisition**; owns **minor forest produce**; can prevent **land alienation**; manages village markets; controls **money-lending**; can **prohibit intoxicants**; recommends **minor mineral** leases.
- At least **half** the seats, and all chairperson posts, are reserved for **STs**.
- Its objectives are self-rule and protecting tribal traditions — **not** creating autonomous regions (UPSC 2013).
- Nodal ministry: the **Ministry of Panchayati Raj**; Andhra Pradesh framed **PESA Rules in 2011**.

## Don't confuse
- **Drinking water** — Eleventh; **water supply** for domestic, industrial and commercial use — Twelfth.
- PESA — **Fifth** Schedule areas; the **Sixth** Schedule has autonomous district councils.

**TL;DR**
- 29 vs 18; fire services, slaughter houses, cattle pounds, vital statistics — urban only.
- PESA: 24 December 1996; ten states incl. AP and Telangana; Gram Sabha powers; no autonomous regions.
keyPoints: The Eleventh Schedule includes minor forest produce, khadi and village industries, non-conventional energy, libraries, markets and fairs and the public distribution system.
The Twelfth Schedule includes fire services, slum improvement, cattle pounds, vital statistics, burials and cremation grounds and regulation of slaughter houses and tanneries.
Drinking water is an Eleventh Schedule item; water supply for domestic, industrial and commercial purposes is a Twelfth Schedule item.
PESA was passed on the Dilip Singh Bhuria Committee's advice and came into force on 24 December 1996 in ten states including Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
Under PESA the Gram Sabha must be consulted before land acquisition, owns minor forest produce, controls money-lending and can prohibit intoxicants.
PESA reserves at least half the seats and all chairperson posts for STs; Andhra Pradesh framed PESA Rules in 2011.

items.title: Part IXA Article by Article — Municipalities, Planning Committees & Urban Bodies
items.body:
## The municipal chapter in detail

**In one line:** Part IXA (Art 243P-243ZG) creates three kinds of municipality, ward committees, reservations, five-year terms and the district and metropolitan planning committees.

**Why it is asked:** 243Q types, 243S ward committees (3 lakh), DPC four-fifths and MPC 10 lakh, and the eight urban body types are favourite statements.

**The story**

### Articles 243P-243ZG
| Article | Rule |
|---|---|
| **243P** | Definitions |
| **243Q** | **Nagar Panchayat** (transitional area), **Municipal Council** (smaller urban area), **Municipal Corporation** (larger urban area); the **Governor** decides using **population, density, revenue, non-agricultural employment** and economic importance; an **industrial township** may be exempted |
| **243R** | Composition — direct election; may add persons with municipal experience (**no vote**), MPs and MLAs |
| **243S** | **Wards Committees** where population is **three lakh or more** |
| **243T** | Reservation for SCs, STs and **one-third** women |
| **243U** | **Five-year** term; election within six months of dissolution |
| **243V** | Disqualifications (minimum age **21**) |
| **243W** | Powers, including **Twelfth Schedule** subjects |
| **243X** | Taxes and funds by state law |
| **243Y** | **State Finance Commission** also reviews municipal finances |
| **243Z** | Audit |
| **243ZA** | **State Election Commission** conducts municipal polls |
| **243ZB** | Application to UTs |
| **243ZC** | Not applicable to Scheduled and tribal areas or the **Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council** area |
| **243ZD** | **District Planning Committee** — at least **four-fifths** of members elected by and from the elected members of the district panchayat and municipalities, in proportion to rural and urban population |
| **243ZE** | **Metropolitan Planning Committee** for areas of **10 lakh** or more; at least **two-thirds** elected by and from municipal members and panchayat chairpersons of the area |
| **243ZF / 243ZG** | Existing laws continue for one year / bar on courts |

### Types of urban bodies
| Body | Point to remember |
|---|---|
| **Municipal Corporation** | Big cities; headed by a **Mayor** |
| **Municipality** | Smaller cities (municipal council, committee or board) |
| **Notified Area Committee** | Fast-growing town; **all members nominated** by the state |
| **Town Area Committee** | Small town; limited functions |
| **Cantonment Board** | Civilian population of a cantonment; under the **Ministry of Defence**, **Cantonments Act, 2006** |
| **Township** | Staff colonies of public enterprises; **no elected members** |
| **Port Trust** | Port areas such as Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai |
| **Special Purpose Agency** | Single-function bodies (housing boards, water boards) |

### Urban history
- First municipal corporation at **Madras (1688)**; **Bombay and Calcutta** corporations in **1726**.
- The **65th Amendment (Nagarpalika) Bill, 1989** failed; the **74th Amendment** came into force on **1 June 1993**.
- Urban local bodies come under the **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs**.

## Don't confuse
- The **Constitution sets no population cut-offs** for the three municipal types; the Governor decides (the source text's "one million" figures are not constitutional).
- **243ZD** DPC — district; **243ZE** MPC — metropolitan area of 10 lakh.

**TL;DR**
- 243Q three types, Governor decides; 243S ward committees at 3 lakh; 243ZD four-fifths; 243ZE 10 lakh, two-thirds.
- Eight urban bodies; cantonments under Defence; Madras 1688; 74th in force 1 June 1993.
keyPoints: Under Article 243Q the Governor classifies an area as a Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council or Municipal Corporation by population, density, revenue and non-agricultural employment.
Article 243S requires Wards Committees in municipalities with a population of three lakh or more.
At least four-fifths of a District Planning Committee are elected by and from the elected members of the district panchayat and municipalities.
A Metropolitan Planning Committee is formed for areas of 10 lakh or more, with at least two-thirds of members elected.
A Notified Area Committee has all members nominated; Cantonment Boards work under the Ministry of Defence and the Cantonments Act 2006; townships have no elected members.
Bombay and Calcutta got municipal corporations in 1726; the 65th Amendment (Nagarpalika) Bill of 1989 failed.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Local Government in Full — Acts, Mandals, Sachivalayams & the 2026 Polls
items.body:
## How Andhra Pradesh runs its villages and towns

**In one line:** AP started Panchayati Raj in **1959**, built the **mandal** tier in the **1980s**, implemented the 73rd Amendment through the **AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994**, added village and ward secretariats in **2019**, and is holding local-body elections in **October-December 2026**.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC asks AP-specific laws, tier heads, the Sachivalayam model and current local-body events.

**The story**

### Laws and tiers
| Year | Step |
|---|---|
| **1959** | **AP Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act** — AP the **second** state to adopt Panchayati Raj (**1 November 1959**) |
| **1985-86** | **N.T. Rama Rao** government replaced taluks and samithis with **mandals** (an idea from the **Ashok Mehta** Committee); **Mandal Praja Parishads** under a **1986** Act |
| **1994** | **AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994** (Act 13 of 1994) gave effect to the **73rd Amendment** |
| **2019** | **Grama and Ward Sachivalayams** from **2 October 2019** |
- Tiers and heads: **Gram Panchayat — Sarpanch** (elected directly by voters); **Mandal Praja Parishad — President** (elected by **MPTC** members); **Zilla Praja Parishad — Chairperson** (elected by **ZPTC** members). MPTCs and ZPTCs are elected **directly**.
- **Women's reservation** in AP local bodies is **50%**; SC/ST seats follow population.
- Urban bodies work mainly under the **AP Municipalities Act, 1965**; **GVMC** (Visakhapatnam) is among the largest corporations.
- The **Panchayat Raj and Rural Development** portfolio is with Deputy CM **Konidela Pawan Kalyan**.
- **PESA, 1996** applies to AP's Fifth Schedule (Agency) areas through the **AP PESA Rules, 2011**.

### Village and ward secretariats
- About **15,004 Grama** and **3,842 Ward Sachivalayams**, each with dedicated staff delivering services at the doorstep; **volunteers** each covered about **50 households**.
- Now called **Swarna Grama** and **Swarna Ward Sachivalayams**; they are an **administrative** layer and do not replace the Gram Sabha or panchayat.

### Districts and the 2026 local-body elections
- AP has **28 districts** since **31 December 2025** (Polavaram and Markapuram newest); the **28 Zilla Praja Parishads** came into effect on **25 September 2026**.
- On **14 October 2026** State Election Commissioner **Anil Chandra Punetha** announced the schedule and the Model Code came into force:

| Poll | Date |
|---|---|
| **Urban local bodies** | **28 October 2026** |
| **MPTC and ZPTC** | **3 November 2026** |
| **Gram panchayats** | **Three phases**, **26 November - 2 December 2026** |

## Don't confuse
- The **Sarpanch** is elected directly; the **MPP President** and **ZPP Chairperson** indirectly.
- AP was **second** (1 November 1959), not first — Rajasthan was first.

**TL;DR**
- 1959 Act → mandals 1985-86 (NTR) → PR Act 1994 → Sachivalayams 2019 (now Swarna).
- 28 ZPPs from 25 September 2026; polls: ULBs 28 October, MPTC/ZPTC 3 November, GPs 26 November-2 December 2026.
keyPoints: AP adopted Panchayati Raj on 1 November 1959 under the AP Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959.
The N.T. Rama Rao government created mandals in 1985-86, and Mandal Praja Parishads were set up under a 1986 Act.
In AP the Sarpanch is directly elected, the MPP President is elected by MPTC members and the ZPP Chairperson by ZPTC members.
AP's village and ward secretariats are now called Swarna Grama and Swarna Ward Sachivalayams; PESA applies in AP through the AP PESA Rules, 2011.
SEC Anil Chandra Punetha announced the 2026 local-body schedule on 14 October 2026: urban local bodies on 28 October, MPTC and ZPTC on 3 November.
Gram panchayat elections in AP are in three phases from 26 November to 2 December 2026.

items.title: For Mains — Panchayati Raj & Local Government
items.body:
Mains (GS-3, clause M3-3: Rural & Urban Local Governance) asks you to **judge** how far the 73rd/74th Amendments delivered real self-government, not to list Article numbers. Build answers on these dimensions.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Promise** | Constitutional third tier; three-tier structure; reserved seats (women one-third → 50% in AP); SEC (243K), SFC (243I); Eleventh/Twelfth Schedules |
| **Gaps** | Devolution of the **3 Fs** (funds, functions, functionaries) is discretionary (Art 243G); thin own-revenue; SFC advice non-binding; staff deputed, not dedicated |
| **Social deficits** | Proxy representation ("Sarpanch-Pati"), elite/line-department capture, MLA/MP interference, weak Gram Sabhas |
| **Significance** | Deepens democracy, local planning, welfare delivery, women's leadership; PESA empowers tribal Gram Sabhas |
| **Way forward** | 2nd ARC "activity mapping", untied funds, separate panchayat cadre (Karnataka), enforceable SFC, capacity-building |

**Data points / reports / schemes to quote**
- **2nd ARC, 6th report** — "Local Governance: An Inspiring Journey into the Future" (subsidiarity, activity mapping).
- **PESA, 1996** — Gram Sabha control over minor forest produce, land and consent in Fifth Schedule areas.
- **SVAMITVA (2020-21)** — drone survey + property cards (Ministry of Panchayati Raj).
- **Finance Commission** grants-in-aid to local bodies (Art 280 reads with Art 243I).
- **District Planning Committee (Art 243ZD)** — consolidates the plans of the panchayats and municipalities in a district into one draft district plan.
- Devolving the **29 Eleventh-Schedule subjects** is left to each State's law (Art 243G says "may"), so the Constitution does **not** make devolution of all 29 mandatory.
- Model States: **Kerala** (People's Plan Campaign) and **Karnataka** (strong devolution, separate cadre).

**AP angle**
AP's **Grama/Ward Sachivalayam + Volunteer model (2 Oct 2019)** is a strong doorstep-delivery innovation, but as an administrative layer it must reinforce — not overshadow — the elected Gram Panchayat/Gram Sabha. AP's **28 Zilla Praja Parishads** (effective 25 Sep 2026, one per district) and **Fifth Schedule PESA areas** give ready State examples.

**Use in answers**
- *Example*: contrast Kerala's People's Plan with the national "3 Fs" shortfall.
- *Quote*: Gandhi's vision of "village republics" (Gram Swaraj) as the aspiration.
- *Diagram idea*: a pyramid — Gram Sabha at the base, Gram Panchayat, Mandal/Block, Zilla Parishad — with "funds + functions + functionaries" as the three supports.
keyPoints: Judge the 73rd/74th Amendments on promise vs the discretionary devolution of the 3 Fs (Art 243G).
Core gaps: thin finances, non-binding SFC, deputed staff, proxy representation and capture.
Quote the 2nd ARC 6th report (activity mapping), PESA 1996 and the SVAMITVA scheme.
Model States Kerala (People's Plan) and Karnataka (separate cadre) show what real devolution achieves.
AP angle: Grama/Ward Sachivalayam (2019) must reinforce, not overshadow, elected panchayats; 28 ZPPs from 25 Sep 2026.
Way forward: untied funds, enforceable SFC, dedicated cadre, stronger Gram Sabhas.
